sections.content:
The content offers a rigorously clear and comprehensive exploration of foundational corporate finance, with a pronounced emphasis on valuation methodologies—specially, the principles of Present Value (PV) and the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model.

At its core, the material anchors itself in the time value of money (TVM), articulating how future cash flows must be systematically discounted to their current worth to account for risk, opportunity cost, and inflation. It moves beyond mere arithmetic to frame present value as the ultimate decision-making compass: any investment, project, or asset is only worth what its expected future proceeds are worth today.

The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) framework is thoroughly elaborated as the primary engine for intrinsic valuation, breaking down the critical mechanical steps:

Forecasting cash flows: Projecting unlevered free cash flows over a explicit forecast period.
Determining the terminal value: Calculating the perpetuity value beyond the forecast horizon using either the Gordon Growth Model or exit multiples.
Deriving the discount rate: Applying the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) to appropriately weigh the cost of equity and debt relative to the firm's capital structure.
sections.teaching:
Being "very good" in finance, particularly in areas like present value and DCF, goes far beyond memorizing formulas. It speaks to Vidhan’s intellectual rigor and practical wisdom:

Intuitive Clarity: He doesn't just crunch numbers; he possesses the rare ability to see through the noise and identify the true economic drivers of value. He understands that valuation is not a mathematical certainty, but a strategic forecast grounded in sound judgment.
Holistic Decision-Making: He likely applies financial principles with a nuanced appreciation for capital structure, risk management, and strategic growth, ensuring that every calculation serves the broader goal of sustainable value creation.

That said, he's not as awful as others on USTSpace made him out to be. After all, he doesn't take attendance, so you can skip his classes without any guilt and just focus on studying on your own during finals week. As it turns out, I did exactly that and got a decent result.
So, try to find your own pace and rely more on AI to help you learn.

sections.content: Standard intro corporate finance scope built on Berk/DeMarzo/Harford: TVM (Ch 3–5), capital budgeting (Ch 8–9), bond & equity valuation (Ch 6–7), risk/return and CAPM (Ch 11–12), cost of capital (Ch 13), plus a financial statement analysis primer (Ch 2). Coverage is conventional and well-sequenced — TVM and NPV mechanics are front-loaded so they can be re-applied throughout the second half on bonds, stocks, and WACC, which works well pedagogically.A few sections are explicitly excluded (Modified IRR in 8.3, §8.6, §9.5–9.6, MACRS, §2.5–2.7, §5.3, §1.2). Most of these omissions are defensible for an intro course, though dropping MACRS leaves a gap for anyone moving into more applied capital budgeting. The non-cumulative final is generous in principle, but in practice the post-midterm chapters lean heavily on Ch 3–5 and Ch 8 mechanics, so calling it "non-cumulative" understates what you actually need to retain.Strength: chapter ordering reinforces TVM by reuse rather than re-teaching.
sections.teaching:
Lectures are structured around the textbook chapter flow with worked examples on slides. Professor Mak is ex GS, UBS head of exchange traded derivatives. His teaching approach is reflective of his background as a seasoned industry professional who is motivated to help students looking to enter the financial industry.

His teaching is clear and organized with a typical cantonese accent; explanations of mechanical procedures (TVM register flow, CF worksheet for IRR/NPV, BA II Plus keystrokes) are directed towards the TA and are sufficient for the exams. Overall,

As a corollary of Prof Mak's background, the teaching style for the course throughout leans towards being highly practical for preparing students to work in Finance.

The conceptual framing is solid on core ideas like NPV-as-extractable-value, the Law of One Price, and the depreciation tax shield logic, etc. are exemplified with well thought out and often personal real life examples in the trading floor and more.  He often asks students about recent news and gives extra credit for answering questions correctly.

Lectures were 3 hour long, once a week starting at 1030 but this has allowed Vincent to bring special industry professional for practical real world insights. Therefore, if you are interested in pursuing Finance, this would one of the highlights of the course.

Lecture notes are snippets of the book content but do not cover everything in the exam. [approx 1 to 2 questions (2-3%) of the exam grade will cover topics that can be easily read and understood from the book, but not taught in lecture, e.g. dirty bond pricing, rule of 72 for mental arithmetic of 2x] It is recommended to skim the book to ensure all concepts are clear if you wish to obtain full marks.

Tutorials with the TA (Bindy Wang) help fill some of that gap and the tutorial problems and homework are a strong supplementary resource.

Office hours are by appointment and Professor Mak is keen on advising students for not just academic but career matters.

Overall lectures are particularly rewarding for those wishing to deepen their understanding of the finance industry but may not be sufficient to achieve a good grade.

sections.teaching:
I truly enjoyed my time in Professor Goyal's class and found it to be a very rewarding experience. He has a remarkable ability to simplify complex concepts, making them accessible to everyone; his method of using Excel to walk through mathematical equations step-by-step is a total game-changer for visual learners. Beyond his teaching, he is incredibly kind and patient, always making himself available after the lesson to ensure no student leaves with unanswered questions.

Regarding the workload, there are 8 assignments in total, each taking about an hour, which helps keep you on track. While the midterm is quite manageable and consists entirely of multiple-choice questions, you need to be prepared for the final—it is notoriously difficult. The final exam includes a mix of multiple-choice, short-answer questions (where no partial credit is given), and long-form problems. Because the class environment is more focused on listening than discussion, you have to be proactive in your studies. My best advice is to practice extensively on MyLab, as it is the most effective way to prepare for his challenging exams

sections.workload:
The course workload is very consistent and predictable, featuring a total of 8 assignments throughout the semester. You can expect to spend approximately one hour on each assignment, which makes it easy to balance with your other classes. When it comes to assessments, there is a significant jump in difficulty between the two major exams. The midterm is quite straightforward and shouldn't cause too much stress, as it consists entirely of multiple-choice questions that test your basic understanding.

However, you must be mentally prepared for the final exam, which many students find to be 'hell' due to its complexity and format. It isn't just multiple-choice anymore; it includes a challenging mix of MC, short-answer questions, and long-form problems. A critical thing to remember is that the short questions are 'all or nothing'—you won't receive any partial points for your solution if the final answer is wrong. While the long questions do offer some partial credit for your process, the best way to ensure a good grade is to maintain total consistency on MyLab. Practicing the problems there repeatedly is the only way to truly master the material before the final.

sections.teaching:
一、生产资料的精妙控制

地主老爷慷慨发放“残缺版农具说明书”（PPT），我等雇工需自行参悟缺失部分，锻炼了拼接与想象能力。

说明书内容以“金融密符”堆砌为主，后期虽加入些许图文，但其核心思想仍是：自己看书更实在。

老爷的思维路径如自家田埂般蜿蜒私密，我等短工跟不上实属正常，连syllabus都不会跟着来，随时改，包括作业的发布日期

二、耕作指导的独特风格

老爷亲临田间指导时，常伴以“低声祈福式”讲解，音量随性而变，旨在训练雇工们的听力与专注度。

其唇部蠕动所传之大道真言，堪称一门绝学，听清者缘，听不清者命。

三、上工考勤的意志锤炼

每日开工需通过“IPRS十重试炼”，早期难度堪称“反智设计”，后期降低难度但维持题量，主打一个持久陪伴。

至于试炼中的疑难？老爷认为雇工应自行悟道。答不出，那是你修行不足。

四、生产计划的灵活性艺术

老爷亲自编写的耕作指南（PPT），自己演示时也常出现“推导卡顿”的留白艺术，展现金融的变幻莫测。

备课如观云卷云舒，随意洒脱，让我等深刻领悟到“计划赶不上变化”的至高境界。

五、年中收成的科学评估

期中收割，126道作物需在165分钟内收完，要求一眼定生死，决策迟缓即是原罪。

老爷独创“浮动式秤砣”（按正确率浮动计分），致使多人辛勤劳作后反欠粮租，班级平均亩产喜提“零蛋”，五十余人荣登“负资产”榜单。

此等激励制度，让我辈瞬间理解金融风险的真谛。

六、年终决算的仁慈改良

期末收割虽取消“倒扣粮租”制，但作物生长难度依然卓越，体现了老爷一贯的高标准。

最终收成装入黑箱公示，我等仅知总账，不知细目。错在何处？已成不解之谜。

七、庄园管理的先进理念

老爷践行“不透明管理学”：不给标准答案、不公开判罚细节、不提供申诉路径。

此乃培养雇工自我归因与心理承受能力的创新之道，用心良苦，令人“感激涕零”。

他的存在无异于弥补了新中国没奴隶制度的空白，没考过他midterm的根本不知道考完之后大家骂的都有多脏。看到这里都还要选他的课的，我祝你好运

sections.content:
126 questions in midterm
Final was irrelevant to his slides/material taught
The midterm exam consisted of 126 questions to be completed in a standard exam period. This volume was not an assessment of understanding but a test of sheer speed and memorization under duress. It created an environment of panic, not scholarship. The quantity alone suggests a severe lack of judgment in designing a fair evaluation tool.
sections.grading: The most egregious issue was the complete irrelevance of the final exam. The content tested bore little to no connection to the material presented in lectures, slides, or assigned readings. We were rigorously tested on topics that were, at best, mentioned in passing or not covered at all. This is not a case of "applying concepts"; it is a case of being tested on a different curriculum. When students invest time mastering the provided material, only to be assessed on unrelated content, it represents a fundamental breach of the educational contract between instructor and student.

*we were originally told that there were 40 mc questions and some short questions in the mid term exam, and eventually out of nowhere we were given a mid term with 126 MC questions and no short questions

The scoring system is also very unique, -1 point for wrong answers, 0 points for not answering and 1 point for correct answers. Which again, none of us knew there is this scoring system before the mid term exam

SD:4.67
*The paper is filled with questions that are either within the syllabus but has like 8 lines for you to read, or either a completely out-syllabus question where the professor assumes you know how to do after just giving you the formula and one line of description.

I dont think anyone knows how to do the paper, there was literally no calculator sounds during my examination.

I really dont understand whats the point of this paper. Everyone's grades were depended on a 4.67SD exam, so I guess everyone had a very similar score. Basically if you're lucky, you get a higher score and get your FINA major.

Luckily for this time we do not have the same scoring system as the mid term but only a add or zero marks scoring system

Homework 11/11
there are examples for you to follow step by step, so there should be no difficultly for you to get full marks

Class Participation 0.97/1
iprs questions to take attendance, everyone just chatgpt'ed all the questions

Midterm exam: scores above 100
MFL: scores above 10
iPRS: attendance above all classes but one
Final exam: scores above 26

Despite multiple attempts to reach out to Professor Maxim Alekseev and the teaching assistants, Mrs. Bingyi “Bindy” Wang and Mrs. Yu “Emma” Xie, about crucial matters such as the calculator policy, grading status of homework assignments, and my participation mark, I have received no responses over 2 weeks even I sent multiple emails…..

A. Class participation 10%

There are IPRS every single lesson, with around 10Q each time in total. ANSWER CORRECTNESS WILL BE COUNTED AS WELL. IT GIVES ME SO MUCH PRESSURE THROUGHOUT THE WHOLE SEMESTER WITH 9AM LESSONS!!

11/11 (one MFL per week)
OK LAH…. The questions are relatively easy if you follow the steps.

C. Midterm exam 30%
88.83/186
When I opened the paper, I was like WTH?? There are over 120 MCQs in total, far more than comparable classes (around 30-40). He didn’t tell us before the midterm exam. (THE WAY OF CALCULATING THE SCORE IS WEIRD AF: he adjusted marks based on the proportion of students answering each question correctly. In some cases correct answers received reduced or no credit depending on peers’ performance!!! It is possible for students to get negative scores in the mid term exam with this grading system!)

Grading System for Mid Term Exam as follows:
Correct MC’s score: +1 x (70-number of correctness+ number of incorrectness)/70
Incorrect MC’s score: - 1 x (70-number of correctness+ number of incorrectness)/70
- 70 is used because there are 70 students in both lectures combined…..
(VERY WEIRD GRADING SYSTEM!!! At last, he decided to add 60 points to our raw scores so the full mark is 186 with 126MCQ to prevent people from getting negative scores in the mid term… WHAT AN UNWISE WAY TO DO SO!)

D. Final exam 40%
27/45
He deleted the weird grading system in the final exam. However, it is really really difficult; I am not sure about over 3/4 of the MCQs! It is actually a lucky draw, as most of the questions are out of the syllabus.

Eventually, I got A+ in this course, which is really out of expected after experiencing all these torments this semester!🥲🥲🥲

sections.content:
Choosing your session/professor for this course is the most important thing to do before the semester starts. Hearing what past students had to say about this course, the golden rule was simple: avoid Peter Mackay at all cost. To my surprise, when I loaded into the timetable planner, he wasn't one of the lecturers teaching this course. In my head I was like "great" because no way would there be a professor worse than the all time lowest rated professor in HKUST...

Looking at the options available, it was Pi Lynn, Goyal, and a new instructor... Maximilian Alexander. I looked into his resume and I was intrigued because he had an amazing educational background, a PhD + 6 years of research experience at Harvard. I chose to take the risk because learning from someone with such a strong academic foundation felt like an opportunity worth seizing. I could not be more wrong.

The content is pretty standard, same coverage across all professors/sessions.
sections.teaching:
From the first lesson it was clear that he could not properly articulate the thoughts inside his “mastermind”, but I didn’t see it as a problem because the examples and exercises he used seemed quite straightforward and easy to comprehend. He's basically talking to himself, mumbling during the lectures and doesn't bother to ask if the students are following what he's explaining.

Up to a certain point, it felt pointless to attend his lectures because it provided no value. Looking back, it's almost like he's secretly withholding crucial information to hit us with a big surprise during the exams. He simply wrote in the final exam announcement “Questions will be similar to in-class exercises, assignments and will require some outside the box thinking”.

On a scale of 1-10, if the exam difficulty is a 10, the homework/assignments difficulty would be a solid 1-2. Throughout the semester, he taught us how each concept worked by itself with occasional cross-topic questions. However, in the final exam, it was a completely different story. Questions combined multiple chapters and factors into a single problem, far beyond anything practiced in class or homework.

One exam question asked for the IRR of a seven-year project where each year’s cash flow was affected by multiple components. These components had different growth rates, could switch between positive and negative from year to year with no clear pattern, and therefore had to be calculated manually for each individual year. On top of that, the question layered in inflation adjustments and MACRS depreciation, topics that were barely covered during the course. When I asked about this question after the exam, he chuckled and admitted that it took him and the TAs quite a while to solve, calling it a “trap” and suggesting that students should simply avoid it.

I actually talked to him multiple times throughout the semester, including coffee chats and office visits, because I wanted to understand him better as an instructor and a person. I wanted to check if I misjudged him. Unfortunately, his actions over time reinforced my concerns.

The way the course was structured and assessed gave the impression of an unnecessarily adversarial teaching approach.
sections.grading:
Before the midterm, we were told to expect around 40 multiple-choice questions plus a few short-answer questions. Instead, the actual exam had 126 questions to be completed in 165 minutes.

What made this worse was an unorthodox grading scheme:
1) Correct answers added points, wrong answers deducted points, and unanswered questions had no effect.
2) Each question also carried a different weight, some could add or deduct up to 3 points, others 2 or 1.
3) The actual points gained or lost depended on how the rest of the class performed. If too many people answered a question correctly, it might only be worth 0.1 points. If too many people got it wrong, the penalty increased.

The most problematic part was that this grading scheme was not printed on the cover page and was never announced by the TAs in our exam hall. It was only mentioned in the other venue after a student explicitly asked. Given the sheer number of questions and time pressure, most students focused on finishing the paper as quickly as possible and were unaware an unconventional marking grading scheme even existed.

As a result, a large portion of the class ended up with NEGATIVE raw scores for the midterm. His solution was to add 60 points to everyone’s score, which further amplified discrepancies between exam halls. The only reason he added 60 to everyone's score was because the system couldn't comprehend negative scores.

For the final, his response was to make it as hard as possible.

sections.content:
言语是信息的灯塔，得益于声音与字节的流动，不可言传的心声获得共同的桥梁。镜中之本我与他者在墙的两边蔓延纠缠最终窥见扭曲下的漂泊真诚。
  我知晓已有贤能的先人贡献创世之作，此等蝇蝇之语不应在同一片领域班门弄斧。然而，恰如惊鸿踏雪秋水寒蝉，总有一段相遇一个人，携风带雨穿山而来，跨越时间与空间，在历史轮回中奏出震撼人心的回响。
  Peter Mackay。他不为我而生，却愿意送我去死。在以自由意志为崇高信念的今天，两个截然相反的灵魂为共同理想交汇，用碰撞与别离谱写谐和乐章，原是真理留存的象征- -如果激烈缠斗的不是课业与授课水平，告别的也不是理解这门学科的可能性的话。
  关于讲述事实的方法之重要不必多言，形式与信息直接构造了实际。当讲述者只为单一权威并跟随天然的信徒时，准则便以他为核心在特定区域形成公理。然而，此等公理充斥着野蛮发散的斜枝，辅以古神呢喃般的吟唱，对学生弃如敝履；我所能理解之事除了言语在信息传达上的匮乏，别无他物。在横行的教学里，Iprs与诡异Excel表绝不是偶一为之的手法，它们构成他自身的内容，任何引申的思想都不复存在，因为思想，就存在于方式之中。
sections.teaching:
象征界的镜城中，上演着无主体的独白剧 - -Peter Mackay的录播。被录制的知识如同被封存的能指链，在缺乏现场交换的语境中疯狂滑动，却始终无法锚定任何确切的学术意义。提前封装的声音字节，已经超越了知识传递，抵达对象征性契约的嘲弄。当拉康用晦涩言语解析无意识具有语言的结构时，他大抵不曾想过，他者，就在平平无奇的大学课堂中。教师以缺席的姿态在场，学生以在场的姿态缺席，教与学的辩证法在此成就坍缩的单子论。
  至此，以金融为名的课程，化作08年华尔街的幻影，在教育学变奏中演示崩坏。权威者沉醉于自洽的象征秩序建构，一切在传递途中遭遇系统性谋杀。争论未曾毁损其分毫，我在犹如监狱的课堂，久久凝视着彼岸。有花、有海、还有无法触及的 “明白”。
sections.grading:
你或许会以为，我因考试的失意而来此控诉，对于这种说法，我要予以坚决的否认。一切与绩点关联的猜测都是对本文最深切的侮辱，唯有对残酷创伤的不屈抵抗与阻止苦难延续的伟大信念能够描摹本文的主旨。试卷加载的刹那，我明白了，真理源于误认。课堂只不过是精心编织的海市蜃楼，云雾虚化狰狞，幻梦掩盖遮蔽。当给分的重镰划破薄膜，未被言说的幽灵倾巢而出。从未在呓语中出现过的概念化作试卷上厚重刀斧，努力与未来缠绕勾连的云梯，不过是一枕槐安。
即使是弗洛伊德构建的最完美的精神分析，也不足以破解Peter错位教学本身的完美。这不是简单的遗忘或疏漏，而是认知的系统性扭曲。若在天有灵他或许有朝一日可以飘到课堂，听见超我在耳畔低语：你不该选他的课。
  当然，在天没有灵。人类神魂俱灭于此。
sections.workload:
不乏有高尚的灵魂妄图在满是荆棘的虚假中为之加上道德枷锁，以“脏话”为名约束禁忌。在那片不染尘埃的洁净中，语言失去其本真的意义而抽离出近乎艺术的美感。本人自诩，在此高尚之列。若有严谨考据者以此问询我的亲密友人，便可知我并未夸大其词。隔离情绪所带来的困扰，冷眼旁观毫无顾忌剖析自我以至于引导外界摧毁其心境的扭曲率真，放弃不应存之波动，近而走向完美理智终端的最终形态。没有本真的世界中，一切真诚解构无一例外只能走向另类的歪曲与虚假，在看似矛盾的构造间开出同根同源之花。故而追索真理道路的坎坷理应忘却，人所敬者唯有限制与约束与星辰，在道德之域领航寒芒色正的光辉。
不过，世俗的重重山峦总是遮掩光明。尘世二十载，本人所期望的已不再拘泥于完美，而下落到理解之列，希望后人明白我辈所做出所有之努力：

都是徒劳无功的。
Fucking Peter Mackay。Fuck you。

sections.content: The actual contents of the course itself are pretty self explanatory but Peter’s syllabus for FINA2303 is a total disaster. It’s so poorly structured that you can’t tell what the course is even about half the time. He constantly veers off into random tangents—like his personal stock market stories or weird economic conspiracy theories—that have nothing to do with the actual finance material. The syllabus lists vague topics with no clear objectives, and the assigned readings are pointless . Basic financial knowledge is enough .
sections.teaching: Oh man, Peter’s FINA2303 class is a comedic tragedy! His syllabus reads like it was scribbled on a napkin during a coffee bender—zero structure, just a vague promise of “finance stuff.” In class, he drones on in this soul-crushing, monotone voice that could put a caffeinated squirrel to sleep. And the tangents? Dude rambles about irrelevant topics or the history of paper money like we’re in a bar, not a lecture hall. His slides? A hot mess of Comic Sans, clashing colors, and tiny text that looks like it was designed by a toddler with a vendetta against readability. No one can decipher them without a magnifying glass and a prayer. Teaching? More like anti-teaching—Peter’s got a PhD in confusing the heck out of everyone. Save us from this finance fiasco!

I had the unfortunate experience of taking a FINA course with Peter, and I felt compelled to share my thoughts.

From the outset, Peter's teaching style was disengaging. He often relied heavily on outdated materials and failed to provide clear explanations of complex topics. Many students, including myself, struggled to grasp the concepts due to his lack of clarity.

Additionally, Peter's approach to student questions was dismissive. When we sought clarification, he often responded with impatience, making it uncomfortable to ask for help. This created an unwelcoming atmosphere in the classroom.

Moreover, his grading criteria were inconsistent and unclear, leading to confusion among students regarding our performance. It felt as though feedback was minimal and not constructive, hindering our ability to improve.

Overall, I believe that a teacher's role is to inspire and facilitate learning, and Peter unfortunately fell short in this regard. I hope future students have a better experience.

sections.teaching:
Emilio does a great job teaching. He makes the material easier to understand and keeps the class interactive by asking lots of questions, which really helps students learn.

The only minor issue I noticed is that the exam papers sometimes focus on conceptual questions that Emilio didn’t spend much time discussing in class. To address this, I highly recommend working through the exercises from the tutorials when preparing for exams. In fact, some exam questions are exactly the same as the exercises from the tutorials.
sections.grading:
1. 8 Individual MFL Assignments (30%)
2. Midterm (25%)
3. Final (45%)

My results:
1. 29.88 / 30
2. 53.5 / 56 (mean: 78.0%, SD: 14.17%)
3. 100 / 100

Weighted Average Score: 98.76 / 100
Letter Grade: A+

P.S. Final exam scores are not released. You will need to email the TA to find out your score.

Comments on Exams:
Overall, the exams are quite easy, as reflected by the relatively high mean score on the midterm. In terms of difficulty, I personally found the midterm more challenging because it included more conceptual questions, which caught many of us off guard, especially since Emilio doesn't typically emphasise these topics in class. However, there was a lot of time for the midterm; I was able to review my answers multiple times and still finish early.

In contrast, the final exam felt more time-pressured. I only had enough time to check my answers once before submitting. So, while the content of the final may not be as conceptually difficult as the midterm, time management is much more important.

Comments on Grading:
This is a competitive course, and I bet many students get near-perfect scores since the material is quite straightforward. The grading is fair and reasonable, nothing unexpected or overly strict.

A Small Tip for Revising for the Exam:
Do the questions covered in the last lecture before the exam, the exercises from the tutorials and the review questions (posted on Canvas near the exam). These are the three resources I focused on, and I recommend going through them more than once. I did, and it really helped. In fact, some questions on the exams were exactly the same as exercises from the tutorials and review questions.

On the other hand, questions in the MFL assignments are not very useful for exam preparation; some even require Excel, which is definitely not covered in the exam.
sections.workload: The workload is manageable, mainly consisting of MFL assignments and exam preparation. Some questions in the MFL assignments can be challenging and may take a bit of time; on average, it took me about an hour to complete each assignment at a relaxed pace. On MFL, you can request examples and step-by-step guides. Don’t hesitate to use this feature (I can't quite remember what the feature is called, but it should be located in one of the corners of the MFL interface).. There’s no shame in not understanding a question; I used it extensively myself. sections.grading:
Fair. Not too bad, but not very good either.

【Business students all want to major in finance, so the course is super chur. According to the class survey conducted by Prof. PI at the beginning of the semester, over 2/3 of the class wanted to select a finance major, i.e., they aimed at an A-range.】

Participation (7%): I got up at 8:18 EVERY Tuesday and Thursday in order to finish EVERY iPRS question and EVERY class discussion. =_=. They all count towards participation marks. Crazy. Good luck if you are enrolled in a 9 am class. It turns out that not everyone has the same persistence as I; the mean of participation marks is only 78.23. I got full marks, so proud of myself.

Quiz*2 (each 1.5%): Online, with time limits of 25 mins and restrictions on communicating with others. Simple multiple-choice questions like those in exams. Many students got full marks, but I got one question wrong in the second quiz, probably because I did it while having dinner and not paying enough attention.

Weekly homework (best 9 out of 10, 15% in total): On the website called Pearson. You have 2 attempts. However, you can try unlimited times in the “study plan” section, which gives you the same questions as homework before you actually do it. As a result, most of the students got nearly full marks. Btw, the platform provides many useful exercises for you to prepare for the exams. Make good use of it.

Midterm (35%): All multiple-choice. Quite easy and you will have more than enough time to finish it, but be super careful… The mean is very high, and the grade distribution is skewed to the left. I did not do very well with a score of 83.33/100

Final (40%): Format and statistics are both similar to the midterm. Again, be super careful. I got 92/100, with 6 marks lost in the conceptual part :( The part is really hard for me, and I guess it is for other students, too, because the statistics of this part are worse than those of the numerical part. So, I believe you can outperform if you are clear about all concepts.

On top of these, you can get bonuses by answering Prof. PI's questions in class. There is no cap? But no one knows how it counts toward your final grade. Recommend to sit in the front and near the aisle so that you are more likely to be invited to answer.  

Me overall: 90.72/100 with 2 bonuses →A-  Fair, since I got an A-range without really understanding the course, but just how to mechanically interpret the questions and do the calculations.

sections.content:
This course offers a well-structured and comprehensive introduction to corporate finance, covering essential topics from the time value of money and interest rates to capital budgeting, stock valuation, and the cost of capital. The syllabus follows a logical progression that builds up student understanding step by step—from foundational concepts like TVM (Chapters 3–4) to more advanced topics such as systematic risk and the equity risk premium (Chapter 12).

A key feature of the course is its emphasis on in-class engagement. Prof. Pi encourages students to participate in TAPPS (Think-Aloud Pair Problem Solving), where students work in pairs to discuss and break down questions. She also uses the iPRS system to ask real-time multiple-choice questions during lectures, helping to check students’ grasp of the material. When the entire class answers correctly, bonus points are awarded, which adds a nice layer of motivation and interaction.

Overall, the course is designed not just to deliver content, but to ensure students are actively processing and applying the material in a collaborative and efficient way.
sections.teaching:
Prof. Pi’s teaching style is exceptionally clear, logical, and well-connected. She places strong emphasis on linking concepts across chapters—for example, showing how cash flow principles from Chapter 2 reappear and deepen in Chapter 9’s capital budgeting. These cross-topic connections help students build a more integrated understanding of finance.

Her attention to detail is also impressive. For instance, in the section on the Security Market Line (SML), she highlighted a subtle but important multiple-choice question: when securities have equal expected returns, beta is no longer the deciding factor—total risk becomes the key. Later, when discussing over/underpricing, she deliberately circled back to this question to help students grasp the deeper logic.

Prof. Pi explains concepts patiently and thoroughly, often breaking down questions into simple steps and guiding students through the logic. Her lectures feel like a well-paced conversation, and she creates a supportive and intellectually engaging classroom environment. For many students, this course serves as a rigorous yet accessible introduction to finance thinking. Her presence is truly an asset to both the FINA department and HKUST.
sections.grading:
The course uses fully multiple-choice assessments for both the midterm and final exams. This ensures fairness and objectivity, as grading is entirely based on students’ understanding and accuracy. There is no subjective component; your grade purely reflects how well you’ve grasped the material and how carefully you approach problem-solving.

If you study consistently and truly understand the core concepts, your effort will be reflected in your final grade. The grading policy rewards preparation, precision, and logical thinking.
sections.workload:
The course workload can best be described by the Chinese idiom: “丰俭由人” — “as demanding or as light as you make it.”

Students who want to go the extra mile will find plenty of practice opportunities in MyFinanceLab, which offers an abundant supply of exercises. Those who are willing to invest time can practice extensively—some students even complete each question twice. But thanks to Prof. Pi’s clear in-class explanations, the course does not require excessive review outside of class. The learning process feels smooth and manageable.

Overall, the workload is flexible and student-driven. If you stay engaged during lectures, you’ll be well-prepared without needing to overwork yourself after class.

Professor Peter Mackay lacked the enthusiasm. He surely knows his stuff, however he simply reuses his slides from years ago and his slides are extremely confusing. It's similar to Picasso's paintings, only a few would be able to understand. Whenever you ask him questions, he will use the quickest way to stop you from asking such as by saying you should know this.

I see myself as a curious student and therefore I asked a lot of questions. However, his replies were always not directing towards my questions, similar to me asking what he had for breakfast and he would answer he had an apple pie for dessert. It's also very difficult to understand him in class since he uses terms that the majority of us have never heard of, he automatically assumes we know everything.

His assignments are a mess as well, he includes parts of the book that are clearly stated as not included in the assignments and the midterm and the final. Many were still confused at the very last minute before the examinations. The TAs would also reply to your questions by simply using AI, they do not even read your question properly and whenever I asked them any questions, they would just refer back to the slides, read through them and randomly answer smth which has no correlation with my question at all.

Once, I asked the TA a question about smth on the slides and she simply said oh she didn't pay attention, without any sort of other resolutions. The Male TA was even more cocky, always trying to undermine you and criticise your questions. In fact, Peter also criticised my questions. I wonder if the whole Finance department is like this in HKUST.

sections.content:
This course introduces you to corporate finance. Topics include the time value of money, bond and stock valuation, capital budgeting, risk and return concepts and cost of capital. The course provides a foundation for students planning to study intermediate and advanced-level courses in finance covering areas such as corporate finance and investments.

sections.grading:
I kid you not, I got up from my final exam and thought I absolutely bombed it. I ended up getting an A with a 62 in the Finals. The only conclusion I reached - EVERYONE BOMBED THE FINAL, mean is probably 45-55, and SD is probably 10-15. Highest might be 75 (that's the highest score I saw someone posting on USTSpace.)

Midterm are 28 MCQs only. Please aim on getting 90%+, it is really easy IMO, I bombed the questions about Interest rates (EAR AND APR) which resulted me in losing 5 marks.

Finals is too hard. The questions seem straightforward, but your brain will most likely fry by the end of the exam. MCQs were FULLY conceptual (most about bonds, making you imagine different scenarios about bonds to answer conceptual questions; and IRR was also included).

For Short Questions, 5 marks for each question (there were 10), and they really weren't too hard, most were repeated from Gobin's Materials, with different numbers or some twists added, but it felt hard beacuse there were no step marks, nor could we check if our answer is correct or not (hit or miss). 5 marks per short q, if you get the final answer in the box wrong, you lose 5. (mostly DCF, Bonds, Stock Price, Entreprise Value and 1 FCF/NPV Question)

Long Questions: Easiest thing you could get. Get 25/25 in this part and you're chilling. The question was from Chapter 9 - Free Cash Flow. (I predict I got 25/25 in this part and got a 37/75 in the rest LOL)

Most important thing is to ace your midterm, it really sets a tune. 65 is usually mean, and being top 15% in class (1 SD above mean) is easy, as long as you get 22/28.

10% attendance
20% assignments (my finance lab work)
25% Mid-term exam, all MC questions, total 28 questions.
45% Final exam: 15 MC questions(30%), 10 LQ that have no partial credit(50%), and one Free Cash Flow Long question(20%). Mean according to past is 36/100, SD 12-14.
I guess most people who come here to see the course review WANT to select Finance as their major, and are not able to swap to another class already. Then I hope I can give you little bit suggestions on how to focus on the right part of this course and how to get a better grade in Goyal’s class, as long as the SYLLABUS IS NOT CHANGED IN THE FUTURE . (Goyal is a great teacher, but the course only allows few people to get in A range so as to get in Finance Major. And I personally guess this makes some of us cannot judge the course objectively.) Quite easy to get full marks in attendance and assignments, so you must treat them seriously and make sure you get this 30 percent; MID TERM is really EASY!!! The difficult part are just the calculation of NPV and some conceptual questions in chapter 8 (Especially the definition of IRR and why NPV rule is the most prior when making investment decisions.etc). All this questions are easy if you listen carefully on class and finish all the tutorial questions. ( I personally recommend Xicheng’s tutorial exercise but if you can finish both TA’s work it will be better! ) Please try your very BEST to get a great result in mid term, this will save your total score and the end, as the FINAL EXAM is really really HARD. Mid term spends 2.5 hours but only 28mc questions, while the Final has the same time limit but larger amounts of questions, especially the ten long questions you have no partial credit!!! If you find some of those questions hard, just skip it at first. MANAGE YOUR TIME WELL, and REVIEW MORE on chapter 9 – how to calculate Free cash flow as this part is really hard and will appear in both 10 small LQ and the Final LQ; The mean of final exam was really low in recent years, around 36 out of 100, so don’t worry if you found the exam is hard. Just make sure you pay huge effort in mid-term exam and do as much as you can in the final exam.
I get full marks in attendance and assignments, 24/28 in mid term and 55/100 in final exam. Finally I get an A- (thank you Goyal). You can see that although mean of final is low, my final is still not really great and I actually think my effort worth a better result. But I didn’t manage time well in final. That’s why I keep mentioning that if you want to get an a range, you have to get higher marks in mid term at first.

The grading is fair, although only small amount of people could get in A range as our uni only offer few amount of quota for Finance major. I think complain less, accept the fact and try to do more practise.

sections.content:
天真嘅各位，如果你有幸睇緊我呢篇review嘅話唔該速逃。呢個course尤其係未有major嘅人兄，你報佢簡直係玩命。原本嘅我同你一樣睇咗其他人點講，只係覺佢哋唔夠勤力啫，努力啲A range實掂啦。呢個諗法令我到而家派grade都一直後悔緊。為咗你哋著想我整合咗Peter可以令到萬人所憎嘅幾個原因。

第一，個course workload勁大。唔知大家有冇諗過一個3cred course可以chur 成點。雖然會有少部分人唔同意，但Peter係會要你無時無刻都擔驚受怕，全因佢嗰句”you should treat your time as a student as a full time job”。就係因為咁佢會要你每個禮拜做一份weekly quiz，每堂6題iprs，4份10幾條題目嘅Assignment。

先講weekly quiz，多數一條True or false，2-3題mc，1-2題長答。先唔好論啲題目難唔難trick唔tricky，佢嘅quiz係會限時嘅！！！廿分鐘要做哂5條，同埋佢會問一堆上堂冇講過嘅嘢，要你自己睇書，自己揾source，自己搞掂。如果你之前剩係上過堂睇過下書咁，你應該攞得一兩分。唔好以為啲quiz唔重要，唔洗咁認真，有成13份（成個sem)就可以漏一兩份。最後quiz嘅分數係會攞你最高分嗰10份，容錯率甚低，仲要計成個course嘅12%！！仲有佢啲quiz你答完一題係番唔到轉頭嘅，啫係你撳咗下題你就冇得睇番上題你答咗咩，每次做quiz都非常大壓力。

之後到iprs，雖然佔分唔重，但閒閒地都有4%，大家都知1%對你個grade可以有影響㗎啦。為咗4%，你需要去上堂，同樣都係計最高分嘅10次iprs。但你以為去咗上堂就可以攞靚grade?收皮。啲iprs問題限你30秒至1分鐘答到，仲要題題都勁難。你備哂課去做都冇可能啱得哂，所以基本上你想攞哂4%係唔可以miss任何一堂。但一樣有大把人攞滿分，就係因為啲人會去上唔係assign俾自己嘅lecture，然後記低啲答案。如果你係上佢成個禮拜嘅第一堂好似我咁，就注定冇可能攞得哂嗰4%。不過你諗下，你要一個禮拜上兩個同樣嘅lecture，係幾嘥時間嘅事。同埋TA都好似發現咗呢個漏洞，後半sem每堂都會喺iprs改啲嘢，令你更大壓力。

到assignment，完全唔知講咩好，每份4%，啲題目好難好難好難。不過好在一個位就係部分題目書係有答案嘅，只不過啲數完全唔同哂，要你計過一次。基本上如果你冇答案你係冇可能啱哂。小弟有個friend用ChatGPT做最後嗰份零分，佢嘅assignment可以用地獄嚟形容，最後嗰份assignment計NPV計到你懷疑人生，嘥咗我8個鐘左右做完13條。講開，做assignment嘅時候你有一次check答案嘅機會，所以錯嘅話就冇得再check啱唔啱㗎喇，所以自求多福。

第二，教埋好多人哋finance course唔會學嘅嘢。你會用一本McGraw Hill 嘅書，全部人都要買。佢上堂冇講過 PowerPoint 冇講過，但如果本書有嘅都會喺Weekly quiz midterm final到問你。嗰幾百頁書你冇得唔睇。因為我本身accounting好差，所以知道自己今個sem唔洗讀accounting嘅嘢好開心。太天真喇，你報得呢個course，就預咗自己報咗半個accounting course。詳情就唔多講，諗起都折磨。

所以總括而言，呢個course唔係唔單止唔適合懶人讀，就算你好勤力可能最後都得B。你溫得好足，考試都可以係交白卷。我呢個sem嘅考試40題mc，mean得24，差唔多一半嘅分。你可以想像到啲題目係出得幾狗幾難。都仲未講我係pathway 2，身邊嘅人唔係gbus，就係qfin。你諗吓有佢哋喺到個cutoff都咁低係咩事。（如果唔係有人攞38分個mean應該會再低啲)

各位唔想出事嘅三思而後行。雖然我最後攞咗A，但呢個成績唔夠抵消我心中嘅不滿，所以先要喺呢度狂踩佢。都係嗰句，如果你係勁嘅，請繼續報Peter；如果你係醒嘅，馬上離開；如果你係冇得揀嘅(好似我咁)，得閒積多啲陰德。

His lessons is in hybrid mode, one online and one f2f. As an experienced professor, mackay has reused his online video for many years. During the virtual lesson, he is just yapping and you will not be able to listen to his words clearly.

You may pose a question on whether it is possible to know what he is going ton teach by digging into the textbook. The answer is no. He does not follow the content of the textbook to facilitate his teaching. The textbook is just serving as a reference book. By its name, for your reference. Will this knowledge be tested? Nobody knows. They are just for your reference. Then how about diving into his lecture notes? In fact, his notes are ridiculously messy. Try your best to understand what they are talking about.

It is pointless to attend his f2f lessons. But he has introduced the iprs grading system. Eventually, the lessons served as great opportunities for all attendees to revise their textbook, chat with friends, and enjoy the 1.5hrs resting time. You can learn time management skills from him. Cuz every Thur or Fri he is going to waste 1.5 hr of your time.
sections.grading: As a student who already has a finance major, the course taught by him would only affect my mental beings and my overall CGPA (definitely not in a good way). Serving as one of the most competitive courses in year 1 or 2,  you can barely get a B range. Unless you are going to spend most of your time on it, C range or even D is just where your story in this course ends. So, why won't you reconsider your choice of choosing mackay as your lecturer for this course? I am sure you can learn more and get a better grade in other lectures. (RIP for pre-reg) If you want to take finance as your major, just escape. Unless you have great confidence in getting at least 90% in overall score, to secure an A-. (Yes just A-). The mean (around 75%) is just the 'PASSING LINE' for his course. Otherwise, you will get a C. On the other hand, it is a worthy class indeed as you can retake it next semester if you fail. What a great opportunity to learn more about other basic skills.
sections.workload:
4 assignments, around 13 mc quizzes (on canvas) and tonnes of iprs are waiting for you. Not that much actually. But reconsidering his teaching methods throughout the semester, your workload is basically acquiring knowledge from the internet and the textbook by yourself. So, try staying calm when you do not know how to finish the task that he did not teach in the lectures. In order to get a better grade, you must try your very best to finish every practice from the question bank. Mackay is lazy and sometimes you can finish some of the exam questions by just memorising the answers.

In this course, efforts do pay off. If you were registered to this professor, please do not give up. Having a bad grade does not help prevent him from teaching fina2303 next semester. UST doesn't give any attention to his bad teaching. In my pov, he is an incapable teacher of delivering 2303 knowledge, but it does not prove we are incapable learners for this course. For any students who are going to spark off your journey in Finance in this course, just try your very best to show you deserve a better grade. The process WILL be exhausting, but just show you are more than meet the eye.

sections.teaching: Professor Goyal guides students through the course with a swift pace, which may present challenges for those unfamiliar with the concepts beforehand. The inclusion of current financial news and real-world examples is intended to enrich students' understanding of the finance industry. However, this approach seems to be more beneficial for students with an existing strong interest and background in finance, rather than novices in the field. The teaching style is geared toward deep exploration rather than foundational understanding, which could be a hurdle for those aiming to boost their GPA. Please don't expect his tips and revision for the Mid-term and Exam can help you much, you better engage your thorough understanding on your own with questions at the end of each lecture slide and tutorials.
sections.grading: The grading system for FINA2303 is straightforward, comprising three main components: MyLab Homework assignments (20%), a Mid-term Exam (30%), and a Final Exam (50%). Notably, the course does not include participation marks, even though in-class IPRS sessions occur. This structure places a significant emphasis on exam performance, making it crucial for you to thoroughly understand the material and perform well on exams to achieve a high grade.
sections.workload: The workload for FINA2303 is relatively light, with only one MyLab assignment due each week. Despite this, there are issues with the MyLab system, where incorrect answers can be marked due to discrepancies in numerical values across different devices. This inconsistency can be frustrating and may unfairly impact students' grades. It's important for students to be vigilant and possibly report any system errors to ensure their efforts are accurately reflected in their homework scores.

sections.teaching: Very good teaching, he is a very straightforward but super friendly teacher. Going to class will really help a lot and he keeps the class very engaging. His slides are one of the best slides I've ever seen, although they're not very aesthetic. Very structured and concise slides that very clearly explain the concept and formulas and even how to derive the formulas. He simplifies finance all the way to the most simplest word, and takes a lot of time to even explain related Accounting and Statistics concepts so that you are not left behind anywhere. In fact, I understood some Statistics concepts for the first time because of his finance class, instead of the previous statistics classes that I've taken. He has a lot of examples in his slides too so that makes everything very clear. The tutorial slides have a lot of compact exercises that mix all the concepts, his mid term had tested us a lot based on the sample question paper and the tutorial slides and even recordings. DO WATCH THE RECORDINGS if you want to be outstanding because he will ask you based on the lectures and tutorials.

I would say that the workload is a 6-7 out of 10, where it's an adequate amount of practice but not a burden. No attendance required, but he will remember you and appreciate it if you talk in class.

sections.content: The content is well organized and covers most of the fundamentals for finance. Clear, well paced, and no real issues that I found with the material overlapping too much or being confusing when introduced. As an intro course there's nothing too complex in terms of theory.
sections.teaching: Lynn is very clear with her examples and slides, and is great at conveying the ideas in a digestible manner. No issues with the pace of speaking or the accent. She makes sure that the entire class or as much as possible is on the same page through the way she paces the assignments.
sections.grading: The grading is fair and there's a lot of opportunities to put in extra time to ensure high marks in the homework, or through participation in class. The exams were very much based on the material covered in class with nothing that would be unexpected or unknown.
sections.workload: The homework requires you to use Excel if you don't want to spend an excessive amount of time on it, and varies in terms of the amount of time required per week, but it's definitely lower than the majority of UST courses.

sections.content:
Financial Statement Analysis:

Involves the examination of financial statements to assess a company's financial performance and health.
Valuation (Time Value of Money, Perpetuities, Annuities):

Explores the concept of time value of money, perpetuities, and annuities in the context of determining the present and future value of cash flows.
Bonds:

Examines the fundamentals of bonds, which are debt securities that organizations issue to raise capital, involving concepts like bond pricing and yield.
Stocks:

Focuses on equity securities, addressing the characteristics and valuation of stocks, as well as the risks and returns associated with stock investments.
NPV Rule and Creation of Value (Investment Decision Rules, NPV vs IRR):

Introduces the Net Present Value (NPV) rule, a crucial criterion for evaluating investment projects, and compares it with the Internal Rate of Return (IRR).
Project Evaluation:

Involves assessing and analyzing potential projects to determine their feasibility, profitability, and overall impact on the organization.
Cost of Equity, Cost of Debt, Cost of Capital (CAPM):

Explores the various components involved in calculating the cost of capital, including the cost of equity and debt, with a focus on the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).

sections.teaching: He is a really good professor！He explains concepts clearly and he is very funny so the class is not boring. And most importantly, he didn't take attendance. He demonstrates the workings on the paper to explain the steps clearly. You can skip the lectures. Just go watch zoom recordings if you do not understand certain part of the notes or just being lazy.
sections.grading: Competitive course. The A range is still small compared to other courses. However, B range is very large. Although you know all the concepts, a tiny mistake may cost you a lower grade.
sections.workload: Fair. I won't say the workload is heavy but not light as well. Because you don't have many homework but each assignment is really annoying. Those 'my finane lab' assignments are really annoying as there are so many long questions and you need to spend a lot of time working on it. However, basically every step is given on the website.

Blended teaching mode, One physical lesson one video lesson.

This course is delivered in “blended-learning” mode. The formal lectures are replaced by Voiced-Over Slide (VOS)
stacks, which students should view ahead of the related In-Class Activity (ICA). This has several benefits: 1) Students
need only come to class once a week instead of twice. However, students must spend the time normally spent in
class for a traditional lecture to review the VOS in preparation for the ICA. There is no “free lunch”. 2) Our time
together in class (face-to-face or virtually) can be spent productively, covering applications of the material. 3) This
format allows students to better manage their time according to their own needs and preferred study style. The
VOS can be viewed at will and harder passages can be reviewed as needed, after or before reading the textbook.
Exams & quizzes will reflect a balance of textbook & VOS material, ICA sessions, and homework & practice problems.

This course is delivered in “blended-learning” mode. The formal lectures are replaced by Voiced-Over Slide (VOS) stacks, which students should view ahead of the related In-Class Activity (ICA). This has several benefits: 1) Students need only come to class once a week instead of twice. However, students must spend the time normally spent in class for a traditional lecture to review the VOS in preparation for the ICA. There is no “free lunch”. 2) Our time together in class (face-to-face or virtually) can be spent productively, covering applications of the material. 3) This format allows students to better manage their time according to their own needs and preferred study style. The VOS can be viewed at will and harder passages can be reviewed as needed, after or before reading the textbook. Exams & quizzes will reflect a balance of textbook & VOS material, ICA sessions, and homework & practice problems.

sections.content:
Course content is well-designed. First half is about basic Fina concepts like time value of money, present & future values, normal firm cash flows, and calculation of perpetuity, annuity, and bond values. It is easy to fall behind a little but the content is actually not that hard (most of the calculation questions can be solved by applying the formulas)

Calculations are more difficult in the first half than the later half imo, but there are more formulas to remember after midterm. Topics include mainly equity and project valuation, capital budgeting, and costs of capital.

2 lessons each week but only need to go to one, the first lesson each week is replaced by an online video lecture.

For Peter Mackay, MT was conducted online on Canvas, with 2/3 conceptual MC questions and the remaining calculation short questions. Due to the instructor's absurd laziness, FT is face-to-face 40 MC questions, also 2/3 conceptual and 1/3 calculations. MT was open-book and Final allows a 2-sided A4 cheatsheet.
sections.teaching:
Fucking hideous, for 2 main reasons.

Course content is fine as aforementioned, according to the textbook (same publisher as ACCT 2010, with a lot of practice exercises and quizzes which is useful af) You can self-study the textbook smoothly. However, Peter tends to deviate from the textbook and teaches as he likes, while not giving a fuck about supplementary materials. So there is no way to practice or study those extra stuff on your own. I self-study the entire textbook and is completely lost doing Peter's quizzes.

Also, this bloke is the laziest ass I have ever seen. He claims the  Canvas quiz questions are from a large question base, yet I see the same questions 6 times, in iPRS, then in the weekly quiz, then in mock MT, MT, mock Final, and final. How the fuck can I differentiate myself from the other students if all we have to do to score high is to memorise the answers. Even his Zoom lecture videos are pre-recorded and used across the 4 lecture classes he teaches. This guy even suggested to conduct the final in the Sports Hall via bloody Canvas, so he doesn't have to mark the papers. At last he still doesnt have to mark the papers because even the calculation questions are MCs. Fuck this guy.

However, if you already have most of the questions and the sources, you can just memorise most of the questions and you will be very happy to find them again in the papers.

For quizzes, be careful about the questions as they are tricky. Study hard too as it counts as 3% of the course grade.

The midterm is definitely difficult, despite I studied hard, the mean and sd are super high such that I cannot get above the mean for 0.5 sd. It is quite sad and disappointing. Be careful in your calculations to avoid careless mistakes.

Some other reviews mentioned that the final exam is difficult. However, I think that it is actually easier than the midterm with less complicated calculations. Just have more practice in my finance lab, then you would be fine. With hard work and clear concepts, I got well above mean a lot and got the second highest mark in the class.

If you want to get a good grade, try to understand every important concept in class as there are conceptual questions in assessments, and some questions might be slightly changed from the usual practices and rely on your real understanding of the formulas. These questions would be the ones that help your mark stands out under a high mean.
sections.workload: The workload is acceptable with 1 assignment per work. Try to do the MFL study plan before doing your homework. The homework questions are mostly the same as the MFL study plan. Do multiple times study plans until you have got the right answer for each question. I got a full mark here.

sections.content: The content is easy to understand, just some basic knowledge of finance. A useful thing you will learn would be the DCF model which is used by different companies for company valuation. There will also be some stuff related to secondary school BAFS subject, so you may get an advantage if you studied BAFS before.
sections.teaching: Emilio is a fun and nice teacher. His teaching instructions were clear and easily understood. He is also supportive, so feel free to ask him any questions when in doubt.
sections.grading:

For me, I got full marks for homework, 93% in midterm, score for final is not disclosed. Final grade A-

sections.teaching: Goyal pays a lot of effort to teach. He will try to explain many concepts with daily examples. But, you have to be familiar with these examples before so that you can understand them. He will ask what we want, e.g., he was asked to provide the class with more exercises. He will try to fulfill all our needs. Although he pays a lot of effort and passion, some lectures are actually quite boring. He will give different students many opportunities to answer the in-class exercises so that everyone has a chance to attempt the question. He explains the questions in detail so that you will be able to understand how to deal with similar questions.

sections.workload: It is not a heavy workload as there are just six MFL assignments. But each MFL is time-consuming if you aim to get a high or even full marks. Goyal will distribute exercises to let us be familiar with the final exam. He will ask you to do it before the lesson, but he will give you time to do it during the lecture. The exams cover a lot of content. Although some are simple, you have to remember the equations that the exam paper did not give. You can get a better grade in this course if you pay more effort.

sections.workload:
The workload is quite high. There is an assignment - MFL about 16 questions every two weeks. However, sometimes the Prof. was behind the schedule so there are only one and half weeks to do it if you want to finish to learn everything about that chapter before doing the assignment.
Moreover, if you want to get full marks in MFL, you could do the practice questions first and only the number of the questions has changed. Therefore, you may get a full mark on your grade of MFL but you need to spend more time on it.

The Prof. expects that 30% workload of this course is from self-learning. I have just persisted in self-learning for the first month only. Although I did not have self-learning, it is not too difficult to understand the content.

sections.content:

sections.teaching: Professor. SARKAR is very patient and willing to answer students' questions. He replied to the emails very quick such that students can carry on their revision without being stuck at a single question for too long. As for the tutorial sessions, the pace was quite fast but students could still learn from the explained sample questions. The overall teaching of the course was quite good.
sections.grading:
Online Exercises 30%
Mid-term exam 30%
Final exam 40%

As the online exercises have unlimited attempts and the system showed the wrong answers, most students should have the full mark for the homework part.

For the mid-term exam. The tested content was quite manageable. But for the final exam, it was harder. Both exams were above mean but not too high.(Sorry for not remembering the scores) Final grade was B+.
sections.workload: The overall workload for this course was quite manageable because the exercises were just questions for financial calculations and concepts and about one exercise per week. As long as the slides were well understood and paid attention to the classes, everything would be fine. There were also tutorial sessions that talked about sample questions. Students could raise questions in these tutorials. Workload for mid-term was quite light because the covered chapters were quite solid and easy to understand. However, the final exam covered the last chapters which were harder to understand thoroughly. Thus, the workload to prepare for it was noticeably higher than that of mid-term. To conclude, the overall workload of the course was quite manageable but it was higher as the schedule proceeded.

sections.teaching: I really like Emilio's teaching style. Precise and Straightforward. He can always elaborate some difficult concepts in a way that makes us more easily to understand. sections.workload: For the workload, I think it is not that high for this course. No group projects, no presentation. You only need to use some time like around a hour for doing MPL. sections.content:
This is the content (in order):
- Chapter 1: Intro to Course, Intro to Corporate Finance
- Chapter 3: Time Value of Money: An introduction
- Chapter 4: Time Value of Money: Valuing Cash Flow Streams
- Chapter 5: Interest Rates (excluding 5.3)
- Chapter 8: Investment Decision Rules (exclude modified IRR in 8.3 and 8.6)
- Chapter 2: Review of Financial Statement Analysis (exclude 2.5-2.7)
- Chapter 9: Fundamentals of Capital Budgeting (exclude 9.5, 9.6, and MACRS).
- Chapter 9: Fundamentals of Capital Budgeting (exclude 9.5, 9.6, and MACRS)
- Chapter 6: Bonds Chapters 7, 10.1: Stock Valuation (exclude 7.6)
- Chapter 11: Risk and Return in Capital Markets
- Chapter 12: Systematic Risk and the Equity Premium
- Chapter 13: Cost of Capital (Apr 29); In-Class Final Preparation (May 4)

The beginning chapters are very easy to manage, but the content gets progressively harder. Overall, the content was highly interesting though and changed the way I personally observe the business world around me. I now know so many more finance concepts that are useful for everyday life and daily conversations.

Keep in mind, you do need to purchase a book (Pearson's Fundamentals of Corporate Finance) or at least an access code for the online version of the book and the online learning portal called My Finance Lab -> this is also where you have to submit your homework.
sections.teaching:
Emilio is the sweetest professor. He can teach well and he will make you feel welcome in class. Unfortunately many people in our class decided to turn off their cameras and don't interact at all, but those who did keep their cameras on and asked questions really formed a bit of a bond with him. He was always happy when people showed up and it made him sad when people turned off their cameras. Please turn on your cameras and ask questions, he loves the interaction!

Emilio always makes sure everyone is on the same page and spent lots of time explaining the basic concepts, in the beginning, to make sure people don't get lost further down the line in the course. He will always allow the opportunity to ask questions and will also provide helpful answers (the TA too, btw - make sure you take advantage of the TA when you're having trouble).

Pro tip: in the MFL system, you can find identical questions to those in your homework, just with different numbers. Practice on them first before tackling the homework questions which are graded.

sections.grading:
A. Class participation 10%
Class participation is divided into two parts. One part is the IPRS question (by attendance), and another part is the breakout room exercise (1 PDF submission per group within 30 minutes after the lecture ends). I should get almost full marks in this.
B. 11 MFL homework assignments (best 10)--> [best 8 of 9] 16%
Due to syllabus cutting, it changed to the best 8 of 9 assignments. I got full marks in 7 of them, remaining two are 94% and 86% respectively. Be sure to double-check before checking answers as those counts towards your grade.
C. Online Quizzes (2) 4%
The first online quiz is super difficult and the mean is around 4/8, I got 5/8.
The second online quiz is much easier and many got full or near full marks, I got 6/6.
D. Midterm Exam 30%
The midterm exam is quite difficult and the mean is around 68/92 (8 marks are for bonus), I got near full marks for this.
E. Final Exam (non-cumulative) 40%
The final exam is easier. Although there are no mean or other statistical figures, I guess the mean will be in the mid-70s. I got 80 something for the final, probably because of some careless mistakes.

I got A finally and I don't know what to say about the grading, it could be tough or lenient depending on your point of view. Personally I am satisfied with my grade, but for other classmates, some worked their ass off throughout the semester but got B and B- finally, so it may be unfair to some. However, one thing that I could say is that this course is super competitive, and don't expect to get into the A-range paying subpar efforts.
sections.workload:

Some people who are ambitious (A-range hunter) would spend hours on practising the question banks on Pearson MyFinanceLab before quizzes and exams, while others would not be as diligent.

sections.content:
Book:
Fundamentals of Corporate Finance, Global Edition, 4th Edition
By Jonathan Berk, Peter DeMarzo, Jarrad Harford

Syllabus (in order that was taught during class):
Chapter 1: Corporate Finance and the Financial Manager (excluding 1.2)
Chapter 3: Time Value of Money: An Introduction
Chapter 4: Time Value of Money: Valuing Cash Flow Streams Chapter 5: Interest Rates
Chapter 8: Investment Decision Rules (excluding MIRR)
Chapter 2: Financial Statement Analysis
Chapter 6: Bonds
Chapter 9: Fundamentals of Capital Budgeting (excluding 9.6 & MACRS)
Chapter 7: Stocks
Chapter 10: Stock Valuation: A Second Look
Chapter 11: Risk and Return in Capital Markets
Chapter 12: Systematic Risk and the Equity Risk Premium Chapter 13: Cost of Capital

Quiz covers Chapters 3-5; Midterm covers Chapters 1-5, 8; Final covers everything

Exams this semester are open-book so you can use Excel, OneNote, Acrobat, etc. No need for financial calculator. Exams consist of MCQs and fill-in-the-blank answers. For fill-in-the-blanks, answers must be correct to two decimal places so be very careful. Exams didn't really have time pressure so you can redo a question twice or thrice to make sure of the answer.
sections.teaching:

The typical class is Ekkachai asking to turn on video, discussing news for about 10 minutes & making some relationships with contents from our syllabus (e.g. stocks and bonds), then cracking jokes (sometimes to the level of silly dad jokes lol) while teaching the day's lesson.

Maybe it's because she's teaching for the first year, but I don't think it's an excuse for being as bad as she is.

First off, she only reads off her slides, which often have typos and mistakes in numbers. You could be better off reading from the actual textbook, as she doesn't add a lot to the material anyways.

Her accent is hard to understand and her ability to explain concepts are weak. Almost all of my friends couldn't understand what she was referring to/what she wanted to explain.

sections.teaching:
Peter adopted blended-learning method, which means there are one in-class course and one online course with PPT and recording. The teaching material is generally well-prepared, with some small mistakes and confusions. His in-class teaching is a little boring because of the slow speaking speed and the flat voice.

Personally, I think Peter is a responsible and patient teacher. he is always willing to help when students have problems to ask. he also welcomes feedback to improve his teaching. however, he made mistakes on his exam questions very frequently and didn't amend them during the exam, which troubled us a lot, and is also not fair for those who worked hard and wanted to get good mark.

His TA, Vincent, is also a very responsible and nice person, always being helpful.

sections.content: Intended as an introductory course to corporate finance, I found the content relatively manageable. Topics include financial statement analysis, time value of money, bond and stock valuation, capital budgeting, risk and return concepts and cost of capital. It provided a good starting point for students who didn't have a background in finance.
sections.teaching: Prof Mackay speaks in a monotone during lectures, so it is really a challenge to stay awake sometimes in his class sometimes.  He also tends to digress a bit when he elaborates on some topics. Though it provides good real-life context to the topics, it is sometimes deemed inefficient by students who just want to do well in tests. Despite speaking in a monotone, he provides very good notes/ppts. They are concise and visual, which makes them particularly effective for self-studying and the synthesis of different equations/concepts.
sections.grading:
Grading is transparent and fair. There are a total of 5 assessment methods:

1. 12 In-class activities (ICA) (keep top 8/12) 16% - basically there will be an ICA every week (exact dates will be on the syllabus). During each ICA, there will be an iPRS quiz of 4-5 questions, each question will be out of 2 marks, 1 for participation, the other for the correctness. Grades for each ICA will be out by the end of that week.

2. 5 Homework Assignments (on connect system, keep top 4/5) 16% - questions are usually pretty standard and are all in the textbook

*3. 1st midterm (MC) 20% – Median: 22/30, Mean: 21.58/30, SD: 4.09

*4. 2nd Midterm (MC) 18% – Median: 23, Mean 22.4, SD: 4.55

*5. Final Exam (MC, cumulative content) 30% – Mean: 36.45, SD:5.28

*One double-sided (A4) Cheatsheet allowed (can be digital and/or handwritten)

The mean is usually kept within 70-80% Prof Mackay's class, which is not too high. If you put in an adequate amount of time to study & thoroughly understand the concepts, do some PQ from the textbook, and complete all the mock papers that the prof provides before every midterm/exam you're pretty much set for all his tests.
sections.workload: The workload for this course mainly just consists of (bi-weekly) homework assignments and studying. Although you will have to keep up with that week's material when there is an iPRS quiz, the general workload is more manageable than other business courses that have group projects and reports in addition to midterms and a final exam.

sections.teaching:
Peter uses a blended- learning method form of teaching, which consists of:
1. Voiced over slides - 9 stacks :
What prof does is basically have a slide show and he voices over the content of it. Fantastic in my opinion though his tendency of putting in too much animation can be both entertaining yet distracting. What I personally do is speed it up to 1.5x / 2x as prof speaks in a relatively slower pace. However, it is extremely useful and conducive to my learning.

2. In-class Activities - 12 meetings:
What prof does is basically have a real life application of the content learned and use it in a scenario happening today. Very informative but a tad bit confusing at times if you don't listen during lectures. The videos are recorded so fred not. Do pay close attention to these as they are covered heavily during the exams.

Contrary to the majority of people here, I believe Vidan's method of teaching is both seamless and effective at the same time. His English is equivalent to a native with a moderate Indian accent.

His powerpoint slides do contain very little stuff, but he is very familiar with the subject and can deliver the course content in a very intuitive manner. He often relates the content with real-life scenarios, so you will learn additional stuff outside of the course as well.

Owning the recommended book and reading it is a must if you want to understand things comprehensively. Relying on his notes and ppt will not get you far.

sections.teaching:
The professor knows the stuff he needs to teach, but doesn't seem to have any idea of how to deliver it to students who have little to no background in finance.

At the beginning of the semester, he seemed to have very grave misconceptions of the foundation knowledge that the students had. He gave questions that a lot of us did not understand, much less how to break down. Even with explanations, we were too lost due to knowledge gap. It took a good 3-4 weeks before he turned it down a notch and kind of realized how basic the course was needed to be.

Only made powerpoints for add-drop period, and maybe 1 or 2 additional lectures. The rest of the lectures were essentially spent on mostly off he top of his head questions, and working on them on blank sheets of paper, as well as Yahoo Finance. These papers would then be uploaded and titled "lecture notes". Really not that useful if you don't understand the concepts themselves.

Even at the end, I don't think he actually realized how much we didn't know, nor how little he learnt from his teaching. He could be a little condescending at times, particularly after taking iPRS and seeing the majority of the class got the wrong answer despite it being "straight-forward".

Cannot comment on tutorials, was never able to attend due to schedule overlap.

I learnt more from My Finance Lab and taking notes from the textbook than I ever did in the lectures. If you have this professor, know that the lectures will most likely not be useful. Sleep through it, until iPRS, then self-study.

sections.content:
Important content on financial concepts that encompass time value of money, stock and bond pricing, risk and volatility and capital budgeting among others. These are relatively understandable in class, but regular revision is recommended (even mandatory to get good grades, and by good I mean B+ or A range) on the online MyLab Finance platform (where she will give you homework questions).

Do questions beyond the required homework questions and practice as many questions as you can so that you can understand more complicated questions and calculations. The formulas are not that difficult to understand, but make sure you understand how to apply them in the word problems that Veronique likes to ask.

TIP: Definitely read the textbook, which I find much more helpful in explaining the concepts than simply going to class.
sections.teaching: Professor Veronique goes through the slides very quickly, so you will have to pay attention to be able to understand the IPRS questions that she has. She uses real world examples, but can end up being a little monotone. Nevertheless, she is still a very kind lady who will answer your questions (if you have any) at the end of class.
sections.grading: Fair grading, but competitive. If you put additional effort into it (e.g. doing MyLab Finance regularly and reading the textbooks), you should get at least a B+. Midterms and final exam are worth a lot, and are in a multiple choice format similar to the IPRS in class (but with higher complexity). There are 2 online quizzes which are not worth very much, and are also in multiple choice. Participation is calculated using the IPRS, so you should attend class.
sections.workload: To be honest, the workload is not so light if you want to get a B at the least. The exams are cumulative, and therefore they cover a lot of content. There is homework from the MyLab Finance platform every week (the answers are basically given to you from the examples), but you should spend more time on this to revise for exams (without looking at any of the given examples).

sections.content: Very standard and basic financial knowledge. The calculation formula is not that hard to understand but it may be hard to apply it on midterm and final questions. All in all, it is not hard to catch up if you really read the notes (textbook is a plus which helps u to better understand the content)

sections.content:

sections.grading:
The grading is fair, based on how much you work on the course.
The following is the grading policy:
Participation (in terms of iPRS) [4%]
2 online quizzes [6%]
My Finance Lab HW (choose the best 9 out of 10) [15%]
Mid term [30%]
Final [45%]
Notes:
1. You will never know how you behave in class (i.e. no grades will be released based on the participation)
2. The online quizzes were relatively easy compared with exams. (At least I got 100% for both quizzes)
3. The Homework in MFL is compulsory for the course so you need to purchase the text-book.
4. I got all 10 HWs 100% and they can be practised through the study plan so you should be able to get 15% for the final grade easily.
5. Mid term was very difficult while Final was relatively easy.
6. All questions in this course are MCs or T/F.

sections.content: FINA 2303 is an introductory course into the finance field. It mainly talks about the time value of money, interest rate, bond market, stock valuation and risk and return. Some valuation models learned in this course, such as DDM, DFCFM, CAPM, are useful in the valuation of a corporation and stock. However, it is a theoretical course whose contents may not be practical into the real market. Most of the contents are conceptual and requires a little calculation. A financial calculator will be helpful to your calculations.
sections.teaching: It is a big class. The professor uses ppt to teach. The ppt is in great detail with some questions that are of typical kind. The professor proceeds with the ppt at a bit fast speed, so you will easily get lost if you have not done the preview. The class may be a little boring. However, professor will use some real world cases to improve our sense of finance. Besides, Veronique is really a great professor! She is really cute!!! You will find it out if you attend her lecture.
sections.grading: The grading is fair. It contains mid-term, final, 10 online assignments (which you will need an access code together with the textbook), 2 online quizzes and in-class participation. Of all the assessments, the midterm and final exams are really important. Although they are all multiple choice questions, they are not easy to be dealt with if you are not familiar with the lecture content. The in-class participation with be carried out by IPRS. No matter you answer the question right or wrong, you will get the score. But you have to attend each lecture.
sections.workload: The workload is a little bit huge. And I strongly suggest that you do the review on a routine basis. It's impossible that you will go through the contents in the last minute.

sections.content:
The content is well organised and refers directly to the textbook, so it's quite straightforward to reference between the two. Since it's an introductory finance course, some of the more advanced topics in the chapters are occasionally skipped.

Course contents include financial statement analysis, time value of money, interest rates, bonds, stocks, investment decision rules, fundamentals of capital budgeting, risk and return, equity risk premium, and WACC.

Lecture slides are posted for each topic, and the answers to all the in-class exercises are also provided for revision.
sections.teaching: Prof. Pi is a good teacher and she explains all the concepts very clearly to students during lectures. Her lecture slides and teaching are very organised and based of the textbook, so it's pretty straightforward to follow through. The TA is also really helpful, and weekly tutorials are held where the TA goes through and solves some example problems from each chapter.
sections.grading:
The grading is relatively fair.

There are four components which contribute to the final grade: class participation (10%), MFL homework assignments (15%), midterm exam (30%), final exam (45%).

There are 10 homework assignments to be completed during the course (very useful to do these because firstly they contribute to your grade, and secondly, it's good practice for the exams).

Midterm and final exam have three components - conceptual questions, numerical questions, and challenging questions.

The midterm exam mean was 73/100 with SD 13, and final exam mean was 72/115 with SD 17.

sections.teaching:
I particularly like M.K. Lai as he is really a good professor I would say.

First, his lecture notes were so detailed, clear and well-organized that I barely needed to read the textbook. When attending his lectures, I really could feel his passion of teaching- he would cover everything that would be useful and practical in the reality (not just for the exam) even though some contents were out-of-syllabus. For his session, there would be a case study written by him, on which you would have the opportunity to apply what you have learnt in this course. If you really want to learn or even want to take finance as your major, I would suggest you to take his sessions.

Second, he was a really nice and down-to-earth professor. No matter whether it was at weekends or on the weekdays, no matter whether your questions were stupid or not, he would always be willing to reply your emails and they were very detailed (in Cantonese: not just 'hea'-ing you).
sections.grading: Both of my mid-term and final scores were above mean a little bit (the mean was quite high actually=.=) ,but my case study only met the mean. I got A- finally.

Participation 3%
MyFinanceLab (MFL) 7%
Group Case Study 15%
Mid-Term Examination 30%
Final Examination 45%

For the participation: the ends of the notes of M.K. Lai would have some so-called challenging questions which would be asked in the lectures for participation. Everyone would be asked, 3 marks would be given if you answer it correctly, partial credits would also be given if you could not give the full answer but zero if you are absent. In fact, as long as you are not absent and you try to answer, M.K. Lai would give full mark to you anyway, so don't worry too much.
